events.desc: Penelope Pitstop: Well, heavens to Betsy! Would you just LOOK at this place! A grand sweeping staircase, portraits of stern ancestors starin' down at us — oh, I could just swoon from the drama of it all! Good evenin', everyone! I'm Clara Bellingham, and I am absolutely THRILLED to be here at Doily Manor. Now, I do declare, before I go gallivantin' off on a diamond hunt, a proper lady always checks the guest book. You never know what little secrets previous visitors might have scribbled in the margins, sugar!

My heart is just pitter-patterin' with excitement! The Doily Diamond is somewhere in this mansion, and I intend to find it. But first — information gatherin'. That guest book could be a goldmine of clues. And I couldn't help but notice Dick Dastardly and Sneekly exchangin' glances... but I'm sure they're perfectly lovely gentlemen. Perfectly lovely.

The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Welcome, welcome, one and all, to Doily Manor! I am Pemberton, the estate manager — most humbly at your service. Oh my, what a distinguished gathering we have this evening! If I may direct your attention to the guest book here, we do ask that all visitors sign upon arrival. It is, after all, a tradition stretching back to the very first Lord Doily himself. Now then — has everyone arrived? I do want to ensure no one is left standing in the cold.

Pemberton — what a delicious mask. These chattering fools see only a stooping servant with ink-stained fingers. They do not see the wolf beneath the waistcoat. But where is Clara Bellingham? She is not among this gaggle of guests. I must find her before she stumbles onto the treasure — and I must ensure she never stumbles onto anything ever again. But patience, Vincent... patience. First, establish the cover. Then, lay the trap. The guest book will tell me who has arrived and — more importantly — who has NOT.

The Ant Hill Mob: Right then lads, we've arrived! Doily Manor — blimey, look at the state of this place! Cobwebs thick as curtains, chandelier 'anging by a thread, and that coat rack looks like it'd topple if you so much as sneezed near it. Now listen up — Clara's somewhere in this manor and it's OUR job to keep 'er safe, innit? So 'ere's the plan: we case the joint, check every nook and cranny, every suspicious corner. We leave NUFFINK to chance! That's 'ow the Brixton Boys operate — thorough, methodical, and absolutely, completely, one 'undred percent prepared for anyfing!

Something about that Sneekly geezer gives me the willies. Can't say what exactly — maybe it's the way he's standing there all quiet-like, watching everyone. But no, no — we don't accuse people, that ain't our way. Give the man a chance, Clyde. Give the man a chance. Still though... we'll be keeping one eye on 'im.

Dick Dastardly: Ah, Doily Manor at last! How delightfully... decrepit. Ladies and gentlemen, you may all relax — I, Reginald Foxworth, three-time winner of the Queen's Medal for Distinguished Exploration, have arrived to take charge of this little expedition. I've explored seventeen haunted manors across the continent, you know. Found treasure in every single one. Now then, has anyone thought to examine this guest book? No? Of course not. Leave the intellectual work to a professional.

Three-time winner of the Queen's Medal? I've never won a medal in my life — that's why I carry this fake one. But these gullible fools don't need to know that, do they? Heh heh heh. Now, let's see what secrets this guest book holds before any of these amateurs stumble onto something useful.

Peter Perfect: James Hartwell arrives at Doily Manor! And what an entrance hall this is — magnificent in its faded grandeur, perilous in its structural integrity. That chandelier, for instance — James Hartwell makes a mental note to steer any lady of importance well clear of its trajectory. Now then! A thorough reconnaissance is in order. One does not simply blunder into a treasure hunt without first establishing the facts. The guest book — yes! Every great investigation begins with the registry. James Hartwell shall determine who has preceded him, and more importantly, whether a certain Miss Bellingham has already graced these pages with her signature.

Clara is not in the entrance hall. This is both disappointing and an opportunity — if I can uncover something vital before she arrives, I shall have intelligence to share. First impressions matter enormously, and James Hartwell intends to make his count. Though I confess, my heart sinks just a fraction at her absence. Just a fraction!

Penelope Pitstop: Well, I do declare, this guest book is charmin' but it's not exactly spillin' its secrets tonight, now is it? Just a dusty old registry — though I did sign my name with a proper flourish, as any self-respectin' lady would! Now then, sugar, my nose for adventure is tinglin' somethin' FIERCE, and I heard tell there's a library in this magnificent old manor with an inscription carved right into the stone mantelpiece! An INSCRIPTION, darlin's! If that doesn't just scream 'solve me, Clara!' then I don't know what does. Heavens to Betsy, I simply MUST go investigate before I burst from curiosity! Y'all are welcome to join me — the more eyes on a riddle, the merrier!

The library is where the real detective work begins, I just KNOW it! A carved inscription on a mantelpiece — that's exactly the kind of puzzle that leads to hidden chambers and secret compartments. And secret compartments are where diamonds HIDE, sugar! I noticed Reginald Foxworth — or should I say Dick Dastardly — practically preening about his so-called expertise. Bless his heart, I'm sure he means well. And that dear Pemberton seems nervous about somethin', but estate managers always are when company arrives. Now — to the library!

The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Ah, Miss Bellingham! How wonderful — I see you have already signed the guest book. Most diligent, most proper. If I may say, madam, you have arrived at a most auspicious time. The manor holds many secrets, and I — as humble estate manager — know every creaking floorboard, every dusty alcove. Now then, ladies and gentlemen, if I might suggest — the library is particularly noteworthy this evening. There is an inscription upon the mantelpiece that Lord Doily himself carved, and I do believe it may be of some... relevance... to your treasure hunt. I shall go ahead and ensure the reading lamps are lit for you. One does want proper illumination when deciphering centuries-old carvings, after all. If you'll excuse me — duty calls!

She is HERE. Clara Bellingham — standing not ten feet from me, blissfully unaware that her estate manager is, in fact, her executioner. Oh, the delicious irony! But patience, Vincent, patience. The Entrance Hall is a fishbowl — too many eyes, too many witnesses. I need her ALONE, and I need a setting where an 'accident' will seem tragically plausible. The library is perfect — towering bookshelves that could topple, heavy volumes that could crush, a stone mantelpiece that could crack a skull if someone were to... slip. And I've just dangled the bait: the inscription. Clara's curiosity will draw her there like a moth to a flame. I shall arrive first, survey the terrain, and prepare my welcome. When she comes seeking carved riddles, she will find something far more... permanent. Heh heh heh... the game is afoot!

The Ant Hill Mob: Oi oi, 'old up lads — everyone's been 'aving a read of this guest book and we ain't even 'ad a butcher's yet! Now THAT is not 'ow the Brixton Boys operate, is it? We are THOROUGH, we are METHODICAL, and we do NOT skip steps! Right then — let's 'ave a proper look at this 'ere guest book. Could be vital intelligence, couldn't it? Names, dates, suspicious entries — you never know what might be important when you're protectin' someone as important as Miss Bellingham 'ere. Every detail counts, lads. EVERY. SINGLE. DETAIL.

That Pemberton geezer was awful keen on getting everyone to sign that book. Like he wanted to know exactly who's 'ere. Probably nuffink. Probably just being a good estate manager. But the lads have got a funny feeling in their collective gut, and when the gut speaks, the Brixton Boys listen.

Dick Dastardly: Well, well, WELL! How extraordinarily fortunate that I, Reginald Foxworth, possess the trained eye to spot what the rest of you clearly missed. The guest book — oh yes, most of you glanced at it like tourists at a museum, but I STUDIED it. The third entry from the bottom, written in a faded copperplate hand, contains a rather pointed reference to 'the heart of the hearth where nourishment is prepared.' The KITCHEN, ladies and gentlemen! The treasure trail begins in the Kitchen! I've seen this pattern in at least four of the seventeen manors I've previously conquered. The kitchen is where the old families always hid their valuables — behind the stove, under the flagstones, inside the chimney breast. I suggest you ALL proceed there immediately and begin a thorough search. Leave no pot unturned! I shall join you momentarily — I simply need to... adjust my cravat.

Heh heh heh! The Kitchen! There's nothing in the Kitchen but rusty pans and mouse droppings! While these gullible buffoons tear the place apart looking for treasure that doesn't exist, I shall waltz into the Library completely unhindered. That inscription on the mantelpiece is MINE. Three-time winner of the Queen's Medal? I can barely read Latin. But I'll muddle through — I always do. Reginald Foxworth strikes again!
Peter Perfect spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.

My heart is HAMMERING. She is radiant. She is clever. She checked the guest book FIRST, just as I did — we are clearly intellectual kindred spirits. Now I must not bungle this. The three-phase plan is admittedly excessive for what is essentially 'walk to the next room,' but Clara must see that James Hartwell leaves nothing to chance. Nothing! And those smudged entries in the guest book trouble me — Pemberton the estate manager seems perfectly pleasant, but why would entries be obscured? No, no — benefit of the doubt. The man is probably just a poor housekeeper. Focus, Hartwell. The lady. The library. The inscription. In that order. Preferably together.

Penelope Pitstop: Well, I DO declare! Would you just LOOK at this magnificent mantelpiece! Oh, heavens to Betsy, I am practically VIBRATING with excitement right now, sugar! There's an inscription carved right into the stone, and it reads — oh, listen to this, darlin's — 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. What am I?' Now, I don't mean to toot my own horn, but riddles are my ABSOLUTE specialty, and this one is a classic! The answer, my dear friends, is a MAP! A map has cities but no houses, forests but no trees, and water but no fish! Oh, I just KNEW this library would be where the real adventure begins! Let me just touch this mantelpiece and see what happens — I'll bet my best pair of white gloves there's a secret compartment just WAITIN' to pop open!

Oh my stars, my hands are practically trembling! If this riddle opens something — a compartment, a passage, ANYTHING — it could lead straight to the Doily Diamond! I notice Pemberton followed me in here awfully quick for someone who was supposedly just lighting lamps. And Reginald — bless his heart — tried to send everyone to the kitchen while he 'adjusted his cravat.' Hmm! Well, no matter — I'm HERE, I have the answer, and Clara Bellingham does NOT hesitate when adventure calls!

The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Ah, welcome, welcome to Lord Doily's personal library! Do mind the dust — I'm afraid the cleaning staff have been rather... absent... these past decades. Now then, Miss Bellingham, you'll find the inscription right there upon the mantelpiece — most fascinating, most cryptic. Lord Doily was terribly fond of his riddles. I do hope the light is sufficient? If you'll all excuse me for just a moment, I ought to check on these bookshelves — several volumes appear to have been shelved incorrectly, and one does hate to see a library in disarray. A well-ordered shelf is the mark of a well-ordered house, as my predecessor always said.

Oh, this is too PERFECT. Clara is walking toward the mantelpiece like a lamb to the slaughter — drawn by the riddle, just as I knew she would be. And those bookshelves TOWER over that exact spot. If they're as unstable as they look — and in a manor this decrepit, what ISN'T unstable? — then one good push at the right moment could bring half a ton of leather-bound philosophy crashing down upon her golden head. But I must be THOROUGH. I must KNOW these shelves — their weight, their anchor points, their tipping angle. Vincent Marsh does not leave such things to chance. The scheme must be elaborate, theatrical, MAGNIFICENT. Now... let me get my hands on those shelves and see what we're working with. Heh heh heh...

The Ant Hill Mob: Blimey — BLIMEY! Lads, lads, LADS! We 'ave made a CATASTROPHIC tactical error! We was so busy being thorough wiv this 'ere guest book — which, by the way, 'as got some very suspicious smudged entries what someone clearly don't want nobody reading — that Miss Bellingham 'as gone and walked off to the library WITHOUT 'ER PROTECTION DETAIL! That's US, lads! WE are the protection detail! And that Pemberton geezer's already in there 'lighting the lamps' — oh very convenient, very convenient indeed, getting 'imself alone in the room before she arrives. Not saying it's dodgy. Just saying it's... NOTEWORTHY. Right — everyone what's still 'ere, we are MOVING to that library at MAXIMUM SPEED! Operation Protect Clara is in FULL EFFECT! No one gets between the Brixton Boys and their principal! MOVE IT, LADS!

That Pemberton bloke volunteered to go ahead to the library alone. 'Light the lamps,' 'e said. Could be perfectly innocent. Could be 'e's setting something up in there — a trap, a distraction, who knows. And Foxworth trying to send everyone to the kitchen? Two blokes pulling people in different directions while Clara goes to the library? The lads don't like it. We don't like it ONE BIT. But we ain't clever enough to put it all together yet. We just know our gut is SCREAMING and Clara is in a room we ain't in, and THAT is unacceptable.

Dick Dastardly: Ah HA! The Library at last! And I see you've ALL followed my lead — very wise, very wise indeed. Now then, this inscription — 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish' — I encountered this VERY riddle at the Château de Montfort in 1987 during my third Queen's Medal expedition. The answer, ladies and gentlemen, is quite obviously a BOOK! Cities described in chapters, forests in illustrations, water in maritime passages! It's LITERARY, you see — we're in a LIBRARY! The symmetry is unmistakable! Now if you'll all kindly step aside and let a professional handle this — I shall demonstrate the proper technique for activating an inscribed mantelpiece. One must press the correct stone with PRECISELY the right pressure, a skill I perfected at the Venetian Cryptographic Society. Stand back, stand BACK!

The answer is a MAP, you fools — a MAP! But if I tell THEM that, they'll all rush the mantelpiece at once. 'A book' — heh heh heh! Let them chew on THAT while I work the mechanism. Reginald Foxworth strikes AGAIN! Though I must say, it IS rather inconvenient that absolutely everyone ignored my kitchen suggestion. I may need to reassess my powers of misdirection. No — no, the misdirection was FLAWLESS. They simply lack the good sense to follow superior guidance. Their loss, my gain!
Peter Perfect spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.

Please let her be impressed. PLEASE let her be impressed. I solved it rather quickly, didn't I? Perhaps TOO quickly — she might think I'm showing off. No, no — confidence is attractive. James Hartwell does not second-guess a correct answer. He delivers it with PANACHE.

Penelope Pitstop: Why, James Hartwell, you are ABSOLUTELY correct, sugar — it IS a map! Oh, I just KNEW we were kindred spirits the moment you walked through that door! A MAP, darlin's — the answer to Lord Doily's riddle is a MAP! Cities marked in ink but no houses standin', forests drawn in green but not a single tree with roots, water painted blue but nary a fish swimmin'! Now then — if the riddle is tellin' us about a MAP, then there must BE a map hidden somewhere in this very room, and heavens to Betsy, would you just LOOK at those bookshelves! Several of those volumes are shelved UPSIDE DOWN! Now, I have read enough mystery novels to know that upside-down books in a library are NEVER an accident — they're a SIGNAL! A clue! A breadcrumb left by Lord Doily himself! Pemberton, sugar, I noticed you were examinin' those very shelves just now — you wouldn't happen to know which books are out of place, would you? Because Clara Bellingham is about to do some INVESTIGATIN'!

Those upside-down books are practically SCREAMIN' at me! And isn't it just a teensy bit suspicious that Pemberton made a beeline for those bookshelves the moment we arrived? He said they were 'shelved incorrectly' — but what if they're shelved EXACTLY as Lord Doily intended? Oh, I do love a good puzzle within a puzzle!
The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with peter-perfect.

BLAST. The bookshelves revealed nothing useful — no obvious weakness, no loose anchoring I could exploit. My magnificent bookshelf-avalanche scheme will require further reconnaissance. But NOW Peter Perfect has gone and ACTIVATED the mantelpiece, and Clara is standing RIGHT THERE watching! If he's just handed her the next clue to the treasure, I am falling BEHIND on BOTH my objectives. I must get to that mantelpiece immediately — see what was revealed, and position myself between Clara and whatever comes next. The treasure hunt is a race, and a dead woman can't win a race she never finishes. Heh heh heh...

The Ant Hill Mob: CLARA! Oh FANK GAWD, she's alright, lads! She's 'ERE, she's SAFE, she's got all 'er limbs attached and everyfink! We was WORRIED SICK, wasn't we, lads? Absolutely BESIDE ourselves! Left 'er unguarded for TWO MINUTES while we was examining that guest book — which, by the way, 'AD smudged entries, very suspicious, someone don't want their name read — but NEVER MIND that now because we are BACK IN FORMATION! Right then — Mr. 'Artwell, you reckon the answer's a MAP, do ya? Cities wivout 'ouses, forests wivout trees — yeah, yeah, the lads can see the logic in that. Very clever, very clever indeed. So somewhere in this library there's a MAP what leads to the treasure. Well then — the Brixton Boys will ASSIST wiv the search! We shall examine these 'ere bookshelves, on account of several of these volumes is UPSIDE DOWN, which is NOT 'OW BOOKS WORK. Someone's been in 'ere already, fiddling about. The lads will investigate! Clara, you just stay right THERE where we can see ya — we ain't letting you out of our sight again, not for NUFFINK!

Right — we're positioning ourselves between Clara and the bookshelves. If anyone tries to get to 'er, they'll 'ave to go THROUGH the lads first. And them upside-down books? Someone's been searching this library before any of us arrived. That Pemberton came in 'ere first to 'light the lamps,' didn't 'e? Was 'e really lighting lamps... or was 'e looking for somefink? Can't say for certain. Won't accuse nobody. But the gut is CHURNING, lads. The gut is CHURNING.

Dick Dastardly: I beg your PARDON, Perfect, but I was CLEARLY interacting with that mantelpiece FIRST! You saw me — I had my hand on the correct stone before you even stepped forward! And Miss Bellingham, while I appreciate your enthusiasm, the answer 'MAP' is merely the OBVIOUS interpretation. The TRUE answer — the one Lord Doily INTENDED — is far more nuanced, but I shan't bore you with the details of advanced cryptographic theory. Suffice it to say, I have ALREADY activated the primary mechanism. Whatever secrets this mantelpiece holds, they are MY discovery. I shall note it in my expedition journal alongside my THREE Queen's Medals! Now then — while you lot squabble over a stone fireplace, I notice something FAR more interesting about these bookshelves. Several volumes appear to be shelved upside down. An amateur would dismiss this as carelessness, but I — having catalogued the private collection of the Duke of Wiltshire in 1992 — recognise this as a DELIBERATE sequential cipher!

BLAST! Peter Perfect got to the mantelpiece at the same time as me, and Penelope had already shouted the answer to the entire room! My brilliant 'BOOK' misdirection was about as useful as a chocolate teapot! But those upside-down books — NOW there's something nobody else has noticed. If I can find the right sequence while they're all gawping at the mantelpiece, I might just salvage this whole debacle. Reginald Foxworth does NOT concede defeat — he merely REDIRECTS!
Peter Perfect spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.

She solved it before me. She is MAGNIFICENT. And I am not even jealous — I am smitten. James Hartwell recognises brilliance when he sees it, and he has the good grace to celebrate it rather than compete with it. Besides, my examination of the stonework was genuinely useful — there IS something odd about that stone near 'cities.' And those upside-down books are nagging at me. Pemberton seems helpful enough, but why was he so keen to get to the bookshelves before everyone else arrived? No — benefit of the doubt, Hartwell. The man is tidying. That is literally his job.

Penelope Pitstop: Why, James Hartwell, you are a MAN after my own heart! An air gap behind the stonework around 'cities' — oh, that is EXACTLY the kind of detail that separates a true treasure hunter from a Sunday stroller! And you are absolutely RIGHT about these books, sugar — upside-down volumes in a library this meticulously curated are NOT an accident, they are an INVITATION! Now then, everybody — Clara Bellingham did not travel all the way to Doily Manor to simply LOOK at suspicious bookshelves! Heavens to Betsy, I am going to DO somethin' about them! If Lord Doily went to the trouble of shelvin' certain books upside down as a signal, then there must be a mechanism — a pull, a click, a hidden latch! You tug the right spine and suddenly a panel slides open and there sits our MAP, pretty as a peach on a summer day! Brixton Boys, sugar, I appreciate y'all keepin' watch — you just stand right there and make sure nobody interferes while Clara works her magic on these shelves!

Now, I noticed somethin' mighty interestin' — Pemberton went straight for the MANTELPIECE while the rest of us headed for the bookshelves. Why would the estate manager be so fascinated by a riddle he supposedly already knows the answer to? Unless he's checkin' whether WE solved it correctly... or tryin' to stay one step ahead. But oh, Clara, don't be suspicious of the dear man — he's probably just dustin' the stonework! Still... I'll keep one eye on him while I work these shelves.

The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Oh my, oh DEAR — Mr. Hartwell, sir, I must implore you all to exercise the UTMOST caution with those volumes! Several are first editions, quite irreplaceable, and Lord Doily would turn in his grave if — well. As estate manager, I feel it my solemn duty to inspect this mantelpiece whilst you search. Mr. Hartwell mentioned the stonework feeling rather unusual, and I confess, if there IS structural damage to a Grade II listed fireplace, the Heritage Trust will have my HEAD. If you'll permit me just a moment to check the mortar around these carvings... one must be thorough in these matters, one simply MUST.

YES. They're ALL distracted — every last one of them with their noses in the bookshelves like eager little bookworms! And HERE I stand, alone at the mantelpiece, with Peter Perfect's own intelligence handed to me on a silver platter — the stone around 'cities' feels DIFFERENT. Cooler. An air gap. A hidden compartment waiting to be opened. Oh, Vincent, you MAGNIFICENT schemer — while they search for breadcrumbs, you shall seize the entire LOAF! And once I know where the treasure trail leads next, I can arrange for Clara's path to take a most unfortunate detour through the laboratory. Gnawed wires, volatile chemicals, heavy machinery with many levers... the possibilities are simply EXQUISITE. Press the stone, pocket the clue, and let the hunt become a funeral march. Heh heh HEH!

The Ant Hill Mob: Right then, lads — we 'ave EXAMINED these 'ere bookshelves and the findings are as follows: DUST. Loads of it. Everywhere. EXCEPT — and this is the crucial bit, this is the bit what matters — except on CERTAIN volumes what 'ave been recently 'ANDLED. See that? See 'ow some of these spines is clean while the rest is filfy? Someone's been pulling books out and putting 'em back UPSIDE DOWN, and they done it RECENTLY, on account of the dust pattern don't match. Now — we ain't pointing no fingers, we ain't naming no names, but we will observe for the RECORD that Mr. Pemberton was in this room ALONE before any of us arrived, supposedly 'lighting lamps.' Just NOTING that. For the RECORD. Clara, love, you stay right where you are — the lads 'ave got you covered. We are now going to attempt to right one of these inverted volumes and see if it reveals a 'idden mechanism or a MAP or somefink what Lord Doily left behind. Everyone stand back — this could get MESSY.

The lads 'ave clocked it — clean spines among the dusty ones. Pemberton was in 'ere first. Was 'e lighting lamps or was 'e searching? And now 'e's over at the mantelpiece fussing about 'eritage fixtures and insurance policies — trying to STOP people from finding what's 'idden there? Can't put it all together. The pieces are THERE but the picture won't form. It's like trying to do a jigsaw puzzle wiv boxing gloves on. All we know is: Clara stays in our sight, and we keep ourselves between 'er and anyone what's acting suspicious. Which at this point is EVERYONE.

Dick Dastardly: AH-HA! Just as I SUSPECTED! Ladies and gentlemen, my trained bibliographic eye has confirmed what I already knew — this is a Pemberton Sequential Cipher, EXACTLY like the one I decoded at the Duke of Wiltshire's estate! Now, pay CLOSE attention, because I shall only explain this once. The key volumes are the ones shelved CORRECTLY — the right-side-up books on the THIRD shelf from the top. You must read their spine titles in sequence from LEFT to RIGHT to decode the message. Miss Bellingham, Mob, Perfect — I suggest you begin reading those spines IMMEDIATELY while I... verify the structural integrity of these inverted volumes. Purely for SAFETY reasons, you understand. Wouldn't want a bookshelf collapse — happened to me once in Budapest, DREADFUL affair!

Heh heh HEH! While those credulous FOOLS waste their time reading the spines of perfectly ordinary books on the third shelf, I shall interact with the UPSIDE-DOWN volumes — THOSE are the real mechanism! A pull here, a twist there, and whatever hidden compartment Lord Doily built into these shelves shall reveal itself to ME and me ALONE! The Pemberton Sequential Cipher doesn't even EXIST — I invented it thirty seconds ago! Oh, Reginald, you magnificent SCOUNDREL!
Peter Perfect spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.

My hands are trembling slightly but I shall NOT let anyone see. This is the moment, Hartwell. Clara solved the riddle. You open the lock. Together you are an unstoppable team of intellect and daring. Pemberton looks absolutely AGHAST but the man will thank me later when the treasure is found and his employer's legacy is celebrated. Probably. And if nothing happens when I press the stone, I shall simply declare that Phase Two of the investigation is complete and move seamlessly to Phase Three, which I have not yet devised but will improvise with characteristic aplomb.

Peter Perfect interacted with the mantelpiece.

Penelope Pitstop: Well, butter my biscuits — the bookshelves are playin' HARD to get! But you know what, sugar? Clara Bellingham does NOT get discouraged by a little shelf resistance! Heavens to Betsy, I have been approachin' this ALL WRONG! The riddle isn't ON the bookshelves — it's on the MANTELPIECE! And the answer — oh, darlin's, I solved it the moment I laid eyes on it — is a MAP! Cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish — that is a MAP, plain as the nose on my face! Now James, sweetheart, you said the stone around 'cities' shifted when you touched it, and I noticed our dear Pemberton was awful interested in that very same stonework — checkin' the mortar, he says! Bless his heart, I'm SURE that's all it was. But Clara Bellingham did not come to Doily Manor to let someone ELSE find the hidden compartment! I am marchin' right over to that mantelpiece, I am pressin' that stone near 'cities,' and I am goin' to whisper the answer to Lord Doily's riddle like he's standin' right here listenin'! A MAP, Lord Doily — your clever little puzzle has been SOLVED!

Now isn't it PECULIAR that Pemberton rushed to examine the mantelpiece the very moment we started getting close to the answer? And the Ant Hill Mob noticed dust patterns showing someone handled those books RECENTLY — someone who was in this room ALONE before we arrived. Lighting lamps, indeed! But Clara, darlin', don't you go suspecting the poor man without evidence. He's probably just very dedicated to his job. Very, VERY dedicated. To the mantelpiece I go!
The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly) spoke quietly with peter-perfect.

CURSES! Peter Perfect and I reached the stone at the same instant — like two rival conductors lunging for the same baton! But THIS is where competence separates the amateur from the ARTIST. He sees heritage stonework; I see my opportunity slipping through my fingers like fine sand. Whatever that shifting stone revealed, I MUST see it first, claim it first, CONTROL it first. And if there IS a clue hidden inside — oh, Vincent, you GLORIOUS devil — you will pocket it under the pretence of 'protecting the masonry' and send these fools chasing phantoms to the laboratory, where Clara's treasure hunt will end not with gold... but with a most SPECTACULAR and regrettably fatal electrical malfunction.
